item.title: College football recruiting: 10 prospects on flip alert before signing day
item.description: Big-name prospects flipping during the early signing period has become less common over the years, but the days leading up to it tell a different story. Coaches aren't only focused on closing out the regular season; they're also making last-minute pitches to players or scheduling last-minute visits to make one final impression. The top players in the country are already committed to their respective programs, but that doesn't mean that they're locked in until they've signed on the dotted line. Who are some of the biggest names to watch heading into the early signing period? More: 2028 football recruiting rankings: USA TODAY Sports' updated top 100 Here are 10 football recruits we're keeping an eye on for possible flip alerts: 5-star DL Jalen Brewster: Texas Tech to LSU No one has been a bigger star in the 2027 recruiting cycle than Brewster, and he's been a long-time commit to Texas Tech, committing to the Red Raiders last October. Now at Buford (GA), while he hasn't locked down his commitment to Texas Tech, that hasn't stopped other programs from taking their shots at him. He remained steadfast in his commitment to Texas Tech even after visits to Florida, LSU, Texas and SMU. The rumor mill once again began to swirl when Brewster showed up in Baton Rouge for LSU's game against Texas on Nov. 14. Nothing has seemingly come from that visit, though, and he's scheduled to return to Lubbock on Thanksgiving for the Red Raiders game against TCU. Other schools have tried, but Texas Tech hasn't given the cycle's top prospect any reason to flip away from his long-time commitment. Prediction: Texas Tech 5-star TE Ahmad Hudson: LSU to Nebraska A five-star in both football and basketball, Hudson was a massive win for LSU on both fronts when he announced his commitment back on May 3. However, Nebraska has remained a constant thorn in the Tigers' side throughout Hudson's recruitment and, at times, has looked like it was in a good spot to flip him. Nebraska wanted to get Hudson back to Lincoln this weekend for its game against Ohio State, but he's instead focusing on a second-round playoff game. That decision not to go could work wonders for LSU. He's visited Baton Rouge every time, and not heading back to Lincoln could be a massive win for Lane Kiffin. item.content:encoded: Big-name prospects flipping during the early signing period has become less common over the years, but the days leading up to it tell a different story. Coaches aren't only focused on closing out the regular season; they're also making last-minute pitches to players or scheduling last-minute visits to make one final impression. The top players in the country are already committed to their respective programs, but that doesn't mean that they're locked in until they've signed on the dotted line. Who are some of the biggest names to watch heading into the early signing period? More: 2028 football recruiting rankings: USA TODAY Sports' updated top 100 Here are 10 football recruits we're keeping an eye on for possible flip alerts: 5-star DL Jalen Brewster: Texas Tech to LSU No one has been a bigger star in the 2027 recruiting cycle than Brewster, and he's been a long-time commit to Texas Tech, committing to the Red Raiders last October. Now at Buford (GA), while he hasn't locked down his commitment to Texas Tech, that hasn't stopped other programs from taking their shots at him. He remained steadfast in his commitment to Texas Tech even after visits to Florida, LSU, Texas and SMU. The rumor mill once again began to swirl when Brewster showed up in Baton Rouge for LSU's game against Texas on Nov. 14. Nothing has seemingly come from that visit, though, and he's scheduled to return to Lubbock on Thanksgiving for the Red Raiders game against TCU. Other schools have tried, but Texas Tech hasn't given the cycle's top prospect any reason to flip away from his long-time commitment. Prediction: Texas Tech 5-star TE Ahmad Hudson: LSU to Nebraska A five-star in both football and basketball, Hudson was a massive win for LSU on both fronts when he announced his commitment back on May 3. However, Nebraska has remained a constant thorn in the Tigers' side throughout Hudson's recruitment and, at times, has looked like it was in a good spot to flip him. Nebraska wanted to get Hudson back to Lincoln this weekend for its game against Ohio State, but he's instead focusing on a second-round playoff game. That decision not to go could work wonders for LSU. He's visited Baton Rouge every time, and not heading back to Lincoln could be a massive win for Lane Kiffin. Prediction: LSU 5-star LB Kaden Henderson: Texas A&M to Notre Dame At one point, it appeared like Texas A&M would run away with the top class in the 2027 cycle with more than 10 five-star commitments. That's cooled off a lot as the season has progressed; A&M has struggled, and numerous flips have occurred. Back in June, the Aggies landed a massive win over Notre Dame when Henderson chose Texas A&M over the Fighting Irish. That loss then did not slow down Marcus Freeman, who has remained a constant in Henderson's recruitment. Notre Dame also got another check when Henderson was in town to see the win over Miami, but his trip to Texas A&M was canceled the following weekend due to the nationwide FAA ground stop. He didn't get to see A&M lose to Tennessee, but it was also a lost opportunity for the Aggies to talk with him in person. Henderson has no trips scheduled for the next few weeks, leaving his decision as one of the biggest questions leading up to the Early Signing Period. Notre Dame hosting him was the biggest win for the program in a few years, and A&M not getting to host him is the difference here, as Notre Dame gets the flip. Prediction: Notre Dame 4-star EDGE Frederick Ards: Texas A&M to South Carolina Losing Ards would be a massive blow for a Texas A&M class trying to hold on to its top prospects after a disastrous season for the Aggies. Florida and South Carolina have remained heavily involved in Ards' recruitment, with each hosting him more than any other school in the cycle. The Gators hosted him on Sept. 26, but South Carolina was the most recent to host him, with Ards traveling to Columbia on Oct. 24. Given how this cycle and season have gone for the Aggies, they'll pull out all the stops to keep Ards and make him a key cog in their rebuild. Prediction: Texas A&M 4-star LB Quinton Cypher: Ohio State to Miami AJ Randle's recent flip from Miami to Notre Dame was a big blow for a Miami class that needed to keep a commitment from a top-100 linebacker. Now they're aiming elsewhere, hoping to fill that gap. Cypher is a player they've been after for some time, and he's even been on campus this fall for a visit. Add in Ohio State's struggles this year and things could be lining up perfectly for the Hurricanes to swoop in and get a much-needed flip of a position of need in an already loaded class. Prediction: Miami 4-star CB Allen Evans: Vanderbilt to Louisville or Ole Miss Vanderbilt scored a major win on June 26, going into Louisville and flipping one of the city's top players away from the Cardinals in Trinity (KY) standout Allen Evans. That June flip hasn't stopped Louisville's pursuit to get him back home, and Ole Miss has also become a major factor in his recruitment in recent months. Given the pursuit of the two schools he's not committed to and Vanderbilt's recent struggles on the field, it's hard to see another flip not coming sometime soon. It's just a matter of which of the two he ends up with. While Allen recently visited Ole Miss in October and November, we like where Jeff Brohm and the Cardinals stand in trying to get him back into what's been another good recruiting class. Prediction: Louisville 4-star EDGE Wyatt Smith: Ohio State to Missouri The four-star edge out of St. Thomas Aquinas (FL) has been a solid pledge to Ohio State for months but Missouri has become an x-factor in his recruitment as of late and he'll be on campus for the final week of the regular season. His dad Justin was once a star at Missouri before he played in the NFL so Smith already has some existing ties to the program but this will be his first trip back as a high-profile prospect. Visits coming this late into the cycle usually spell disaster for the team that isn't getting the chance to make one last impression. Given that the Buckeyes just lost a commitment from five-star DJ Jacobs and things seem to be in limbo in Columbus, Missouri's in a good spot to pull off a shocker. Prediction: Missouri 4-star WR Jaden Upshaw: Texas A&M to Georgia Upshaw is another Aggie commit who may not be committed in the coming weeks due to the team's success this year, along with not being in town on Nov. 14 because of the nationwide ground stop. He's been committed since early in the year and has remained committed despite pushes from programs like Alabama and Georgia. Finding a way to keep Upshaw at home appears to be a priority for Kirby Smart, while Alabama tried to get him to Tuscaloosa for the Iron Bowl. However, Upshaw recently announced that he would not be heading to that game. The last few weeks of the season could play a factor in Upshaw's decision. Georgia has been the top team in college football this year and is once again recruiting well. If Smart pushes hard enough to close the deal, don't be shocked to see Upshaw in Athens next year. Prediction: Georgia 4-star EDGE Chris Whitehead: LSU to Virginia Tech Virginia Tech missed out on Whitehead, the state's top player, when he announced his commitment to LSU in June. That hasn't stopped James Franklin and the Hokies from trying to land a massive recruiting win before the Early Signing Period. Whitehead's visited Blacksburg and Baton Rouge multiple times, giving each program a chance to make a lasting impression. Virginia Tech has taken a good step forward as a program in Franklin's first year, and LSU has struggled under Kiffin in Year 1, but it's hard to determine whether the first year at each program has had any impact on Whitehead's decision. Until he says otherwise, LSU remains in the driver's seat here. Prediction: LSU 3-star QB Jaden Jefferson: Hawaii to Arizona State Many may not have realized it back in April when Jefferson co

item.title: Ryan Clark says Aaron Rodgers’ legacy isn’t tarnished because it was ‘never built on character’
item.description: Credit: The Pivot, ESPN The final act of Aaron Rodgers’ career took a pretty shocking turn this week. The future Hall of Famer was unceremoniously benched via a social media post late Tuesday night with little explanation. In response, he showed up on The Pat McAfee Show on Wednesday and threw his longtime coach Mike McCarthy under the bus, accusing him of falling asleep in meetings and several other shortcomings in his first year in Pittsburgh. We’ve seen great players leave the league far from their peak. Tom Brady got his last Super Bowl with the Buccaneers, but his final season in Tampa Bay was far from pretty. But nothing in that final season affected Brady’s status amongst the all-time greats. Given Rodgers’ exit was so loud, and according to many former pros , so against the unwritten rules of football life , will Rodgers see his reputation take a hit due to how this chapter ends? Ryan Clark doesn’t think so. Speaking on his show The Pivot , Clark, who has been public with his feelings about Rodgers for some time, argued that the quarterback’s legacy as a player was safe, because it was never tied to him being a good guy. “Aaron Rodgers’ legacy is in no way tarnished, because his legacy was never built on character,” Clark said. “If Tom Brady says this when leaving the New England Patriots, we’re shocked. We’re surprised. Because it’s against everything he’s ever shown us. Mike McCarthy should’ve known that kissing a rattlesnake was safer than coaching Aaron Rodgers again. He’s shown many times there’s no loyalty, there’s nothing I won’t say, I won’t think about the person I’m talking about before I think about myself. Many people will say that he fell on the sword. That this was about the team. Well, you’re already out of the building. This is about you.” Clark noted that the fact that Rodgers’ former teammates were forced to answer so many questions about his departure was proof that his actions weren’t about helping the team. “Aaron Rodgers didn’t do that to be some sort of martyr. Aaron Rodgers did that because he got demoted and said, ‘Oh, I’m going to get you way more than you could get me.'” From there, Clark lamented what has become of his former team , arguing that he was against the hiring of McCarthy in the first place as it went against what the Steelers usually looked for in a coach. “Aaron Rodgers’ legacy isn’t tarnished, because it was never built on character” Multiple things can be true at once. Aaron Rodgers can be both right & wrong. Telling the truth doesn’t preclude you from being disingenuous, & Mike McCarthy can have a winning record while operating like a bad head coach. Regardless of where you stand, one thing is fundamentally clear: The Pittsburgh Steelers have a problem so deeply rooted that they may need to tear it all down to fix it. @thepivotsports on @thepivot @youtube #ThePivotSports #ThePivot #Steelers #AaronRodgers https://t.co/1j2kEwzC58 — Ryan Clark (@Realrclark25) November 27, 2026 Clark ultimately come

Rodgers probably had some points about how things were going with McCarthy , but to think that he was not also part of the problem is ridiculous, and to think that Rodgers’ decision to go public was out of team loyalty rather than a desire to win a personal vendetta is a strain at best. item.title: Bears Week 12 Flashbacks: Arrowhead Upset, Hester’s Magic, Turkey Day
item.description: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 25: Cairo Santos #2 of the Chicago Bears lines up a field goal attempt in the second quarter against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 25, 2021 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this week’s edition of the Gridiron Time Machine, we’re revisiting an unlikely comeback at Arrowhead, a valuable lesson in why you should never kick to Devin Hester, and a Thanksgiving victory that came down to the final second. So hop aboard the time machine for another fantastic trip down memory lane. 1.) 1993, Bears @ Chiefs: An unlikely comeback at Arrowhead November 21, 1993 | Bears win 19-17 The Bears entered Week 12 of the 1993 season with a 4-5 record under first-year head coach Dave Wannstedt. A trip to Arrowhead Stadium to face the 7-2 Kansas City Chiefs wasn’t exactly the ideal opportunity to get back to .500. Things certainly didn’t look promising early on, as future Hall of Fame running back Marcus Allen found the end zone twice to give Kansas City a 14-0 lead in the second quarter. The Bears managed to get on the board before halftime thanks to a pair of Kevin Butler field goals from 32 and 45 yards out, cutting the deficit to eight. Chicago continued chipping away in the third quarter when Tim Worley broke loose for a 25-yard touchdown run. A blocked extra point kept the Bears from pulling within one, and a Nick Lowery field goal extended Kansas City’s lead to 17-12 heading into the fourth quarter. If you were expecting Jim Harbaugh to lead some sort of aerial assault to complete the comeback, think again. Harbaugh completed 13 of his 20 pass attempts for just 98 yards and two interceptions, finishing the afternoon with a passer rating of 37.1. He was considerably more effective with his legs, rushing for 56 yards on eight attempts. The Bears leaned heavily on their ground game, rushing for 185 yards on 43 attempts. Worley led the way with 59 yards, while Neal Anderson added another 42. With just over three minutes remaining, Anderson punched it in from one yard out to give Chicago its first lead of the afternoon. The Bears’ defense, which recorded five sacks and held Kansas City to just three second-half points, made sure that lead stuck. The Chiefs would go on to win the AFC West and reach the AFC Championship Game that season, but on this particular Sunday, the Bears had their number. Winning on the road against one of the AFC’s best teams without throwing for 100 yards? That’s some Chicago Bears football right there. 2.) 2007, Bears vs. Broncos: Denver learns not to kick to Hester November 25, 2007 | Bears win 37-34 (OT) Coming off their Super Bowl appearance the previous season, the 2007 Chicago Bears found themselves sitting at 4-6 entering Week 12. item.content:encoded: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 25: Cairo Santos #2 of the Chicago Bears lines up a field goal attempt in the second quarter against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 25, 2021 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this week’s edition of the Gridiron Time Machine, we’re revisiting an unlikely comeback at Arrowhead, a valuable lesson in why you should never kick to Devin Hester, and a Thanksgiving victory that came down to the final second. So hop aboard the time machine for another fantastic trip down memory lane. 1.) 1993, Bears @ Chiefs: An unlikely comeback at Arrowhead November 21, 1993 | Bears win 19-17 The Bears entered Week 12 of the 1993 season with a 4-5 record under first-year head coach Dave Wannstedt. A trip to Arrowhead Stadium to face the 7-2 Kansas City Chiefs wasn’t exactly the ideal opportunity to get back to .500. Things certainly didn’t look promising early on, as future Hall of Fame running back Marcus Allen found the end zone twice to give Kansas City a 14-0 lead in the second quarter. The Bears managed to get on the board before halftime thanks to a pair of Kevin Butler field goals from 32 and 45 yards out, cutting the deficit to eight. Chicago continued chipping away in the third quarter when Tim Worley broke loose for a 25-yard touchdown run. A blocked extra point kept the Bears from pulling within one, and a Nick Lowery field goal extended Kansas City’s lead to 17-12 heading into the fourth quarter. If you were expecting Jim Harbaugh to lead some sort of aerial assault to complete the comeback, think again. Harbaugh completed 13 of his 20 pass attempts for just 98 yards and two interceptions, finishing the afternoon with a passer rating of 37.1. He was considerably more effective with his legs, rushing for 56 yards on eight attempts. The Bears leaned heavily on their ground game, rushing for 185 yards on 43 attempts. Worley led the way with 59 yards, while Neal Anderson added another 42. With just over three minutes remaining, Anderson punched it in from one yard out to give Chicago its first lead of the afternoon. The Bears’ defense, which recorded five sacks and held Kansas City to just three second-half points, made sure that lead stuck. The Chiefs would go on to win the AFC West and reach the AFC Championship Game that season, but on this particular Sunday, the Bears had their number. Winning on the road against one of the AFC’s best teams without throwing for 100 yards? That’s some Chicago Bears football right there. 2.) 2007, Bears vs. Broncos: Denver learns not to kick to Hester November 25, 2007 | Bears win 37-34 (OT) Coming off their Super Bowl appearance the previous season, the 2007 Chicago Bears found themselves sitting at 4-6 entering Week 12. While the season hadn’t gone according to plan, the Bears still had one of the most electrifying players in football at their disposal. Apparently, Denver Broncos punter Todd Sauerbrun wasn’t particularly concerned. Leading up to the game, Sauerbrun made it known that the Broncos weren’t planning on kicking away from Devin Hester. You can probably guess where this is going. Trailing 13-6 early in the third quarter, Hester fielded a Sauerbrun punt and returned it 75 yards for a touchdown, tying the game at 13. Denver eventually regained the lead on a five-yard touchdown run by Cecil Sapp, setting up another opportunity for Hester on the ensuing kickoff. This time, he took it 88 yards to the house. Two return touchdowns in the same quarter, covering a combined 163 yards. Perhaps kicking away from Hester wasn’t such a bad idea after all. Despite Hester’s heroics, the Bears still found themselves trailing 34-20 in the fourth quarter. A young quarterback by the name of Jay Cutler was having himself quite an afternoon, completing 17 of 31 passes for 302 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. Yes, that Jay Cutler. Adrian Peterson cut Denver’s lead to seven with a four-yard touchdown run before the Bears’ special teams came through again, blocking a punt and giving Chicago another opportunity to tie the game. With 28 seconds remaining, Rex Grossman connected with Bernard Berrian for a three-yard touchdown to send the game into overtime. Robbie Gould put the finishing touches on the comeback with a 39-yard field goal, giving Chicago a 37-34 victory. The Bears won despite committing four turnovers and surrendering 430 yards of total offense. Of course, it helps when arguably the greatest return specialist in NFL history is spotting your offense 14 points. Lesson learned, Denver. 3.) 2021, Bears @ Lions: Santos saves Thanksgiving November 25, 2021 | Bears win 16-14 There wasn’t much for either team to be thankful for heading into this Thanksgiving Day matchup. The Bears were riding a five-game losing streak, while the Detroit Lions were still searching for their first victory under head coach Dan Campbell. With rookie quarterback Justin Fields sidelined by a rib injury, veteran Andy Dalton got the starting nod for Chicago. Detroit struck first when Jared Goff connected with Josh Reynolds for a 39-yard touchdown in the opening quarter. The Bears responded with 13 unanswered points in the second quarter, highlighted by a 17-yard touchdown pass from Dalton to Jimmy Graham. Goff helped Detroit reclaim the lead late in the third quarter, finding T.J. Hockenson for a 17-yard touchdown to put the Lions ahead 14-13. What followed was a rather impressive display of clock management by the Bears. Taking possession with 8:30 remaining in the fourth quarter, Chicago methodically worked its way down the field. Dalton connected with Damiere Byrd for a pair of crucial third-down conversions, the second of which came after Detroit was penalized for calling consecutive timeouts. Byrd’s seven-yard reception gave Chicago a first down at the Detroit four-yard line, allowing the Bears to kneel three times and leave just one second on the clock. Watch the full game highlights on YouTube by clicking below: Cairo Santos stepped onto the field and connected on a 28-yard field goal as time expired, capping an 18-play, 69-yard drive that consumed the final 8:30 of regulation. Lost in the excitement of the game-winning drive was a pretty solid performance from Dalton, who completed 24 of 39 passes for 317 yards, a touchdown and an interception. Darnell Mooney accounted for 123 of those yards on just five receptions, while Santos converted all three of his field goal attempts. The Bears snapped their five-game losing streak and improved to 4-7, while the Lions fell to 0-10-1. It wasn’t the prettiest Thanksgiving Day football game you’ll ever see, but the Bears walked away with a victory over a division rival. And Bears fans could finally enjoy their Thanksgiving dinner without a side of disappointment. Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs .

item.title: Tiger Tails: LSU men’s basketball is on a roll
item.description: SPOKANE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 14: Head coach Will Wade of the LSU Tigers speaks to the media after the game against the Gonzaga bulldogs at Spokane Numerica Veterans Arena on November 14, 2026 in Spokane, Washington. (Photo by Mitchell Scaglione/LSU/University Images via Getty Images) Welcome to Tiger Tales, a daily roundup of LSU and college sports news! It’s been a while since LSU men’s basketball has been great- even good- but we’re finally back. Will Wade’s return brought hype, but I’m not sure anyone expected this kind of impact right away, and even though the games have been close, the Tigers are undefeated. item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: Jameis Winston, J.J. McCarthy, playoffs, more
item.description: Michael Buscemi asks: Really curious about this question and answer at least in every game there is a few times a cornerback or safety drops an interception do they ever have drills for defensive backs from quarterbacks that train their hands better to catch and making deceptions it happened so often I’m just curious to see what your answer is about practicing drills to help control the ball. Ed says: Michael, these guys are at the highest level of their sport. They practice catching the ball every day — or at least every day there is a practice. There are always drills that involve catching the ball, both standing still and on the move. There is also a JUGS machine guys can use at the end of practice. Several players use it all the time. Reality is, though, game and practice conditions are much different. You practice the fundamentals of catching so that it becomes muscle memory, but you can’t mimic game speed or circumstances. John Steinbreder asks: As is the case with so many Giants fans, I am enjoying every part of the Jameis Winston Experience and the deft and very selfless ways he has been performing his duties as QB2 for the Giants. And that has me wondering: has there ever been a back-up quite like him? The thoughtful mentoring of the young signal callers. Coming in off the bench when needed to win games. And now his role as the man orchestrating the tush-push, whether as a runner or passer. Then, of course, there are the signals he actually calls, in part to try and draw the opposing team offsides and also to entertain. And his barking, “Who Let The Dogs Out” in the Commanders game still has me chortling weeks later. I am also curious as to your thoughts on Harbaugh utilizing Jameis in those situations as a way of protecting JJ from taking unnecessary shots. It makes me think back to Tom Coughlin who never called QB sneaks with Eli because he did not want to expose him unnecessarily to injury. It’s a pretty smart move on Harbaugh’s part, to protect JJ and also to keep Jameis engaged and involved. Ed says: John, there have been many veteran backup quarterbacks over the years who have willingly helped younger players learn their craft. There have been backups/journeymen with flamboyant personalities like Ryan Fitzpatrick. Winston, though, is one of a kind. He willingly embraced helping Jaxson Dart. Even after J.J. McCarthy was given his starting job, Winston has embraced doing everything he can to help McCarthy and the team as a whole. This guy is a team captain, a member of the team’s leadership council and the guy who breaks down the team’s pre-game on-field huddle. I don’t know of a backup quarterback who has carried that kind of respect from his teammates. As for the QB sneak stuff, I think there are two parts to it. I think it is something that Winston does well — not all quarterbacks have the feel for it, or really want to throw themselves into that scrum. Ed says: Michael, these guys are at the highest level of their sport. They practice catching the ball every day — or at least every day there is a practice. There are always drills that involve catching the ball, both standing still and on the move. There is also a JUGS machine guys can use at the end of practice. Several players use it all the time. Reality is, though, game and practice conditions are much different. You practice the fundamentals of catching so that it becomes muscle memory, but you can’t mimic game speed or circumstances. John Steinbreder asks: As is the case with so many Giants fans, I am enjoying every part of the Jameis Winston Experience and the deft and very selfless ways he has been performing his duties as QB2 for the Giants. And that has me wondering: has there ever been a back-up quite like him? The thoughtful mentoring of the young signal callers. Coming in off the bench when needed to win games. And now his role as the man orchestrating the tush-push, whether as a runner or passer. Then, of course, there are the signals he actually calls, in part to try and draw the opposing team offsides and also to entertain. And his barking, “Who Let The Dogs Out” in the Commanders game still has me chortling weeks later. I am also curious as to your thoughts on Harbaugh utilizing Jameis in those situations as a way of protecting JJ from taking unnecessary shots. It makes me think back to Tom Coughlin who never called QB sneaks with Eli because he did not want to expose him unnecessarily to injury. It’s a pretty smart move on Harbaugh’s part, to protect JJ and also to keep Jameis engaged and involved. Ed says: John, there have been many veteran backup quarterbacks over the years who have willingly helped younger players learn their craft. There have been backups/journeymen with flamboyant personalities like Ryan Fitzpatrick. Winston, though, is one of a kind. He willingly embraced helping Jaxson Dart. Even after J.J. McCarthy was given his starting job, Winston has embraced doing everything he can to help McCarthy and the team as a whole. This guy is a team captain, a member of the team’s leadership council and the guy who breaks down the team’s pre-game on-field huddle. I don’t know of a backup quarterback who has carried that kind of respect from his teammates. As for the QB sneak stuff, I think there are two parts to it. I think it is something that Winston does well — not all quarterbacks have the feel for it, or really want to throw themselves into that scrum. Also, Harbaugh likes to find some type of role for everyone on the game day roster. John Harbaugh answered a question about Winston and the QB sneaks on Friday. “He’s good at it,” Harbaugh said. “I think originally, probably, it was something he had been repping already, and so it was one less thing on J.J.’s (quarterback J.J. McCarthy) plate. Just being honest, I’d probably say that was kind of where we started with it. We kind of got to the point where if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. It’s been good for us. It ends up being a whole package for us.” Paul Staunton asks: At this point, what percentage of the Giants’ playbook can the OC use when JJ is in the game? Ed says: Paul, my understanding is that there are no limitations at this point. Now, you also have to understand that there are dozens of plays, if not more than that, in the playbook that will never get used. But, the point is the Giants are not limited by McCarthy’s knowledge at this point. Thomas Fergus asks: What is going on with Darius Alexander? Many of us had high expectations of him contributing to the defense this year. He flashed strong play and now is invisible and getting healthy scratched. Has he lost the trust of Wilson? We need all hands on deck for the playoffs, will Alexander get on the field at any point left this year? Ed says: Thomas, the fact that Alexander was not active last Sunday against the Jacksonville Jaguars was curious. C.J. Okoye got a uniform instead of Alexander against the Jacksonville Jaguars, and had a nice game. It could have been as simple as the Giants feeling that Okoye had a really nice week of practice and deserved to play. If that was the case, he rewarded them. Alexander had been trending up, but his play vs. Washington in Week 10 wasn’t good. Perhaps not getting a uniform was a message. He will play when the coaching staff believes he deserves to play. James Pauloski asks: Last week Kayvon Thibideaux intercepted a pass on an attempted two point conversion. Why isn’t that recorded as an interception by him? Ed says: The play is scored as an extra-point try, not an offensive or defensive play. No stats are recorded. Players don’t get credit for pass completetions/catches/rushing yards/tackles, or anything else. Thibodeaux chose not to run the ball out of the end zone. Had he returned it all the way for a score, it would have been two points for the Giants. Vincent Moody asks: Hi, one thing I was wondering about. The Giants O- line hasn’t been good at all, especially at run-blocking. The Eagles moved on from Jeff Stoutland recently. Is he retired or is there any chance he would come over to the Giants. Ed says: Vincent, first I am going to strongly disagree with the notion that the offensive line “hasn’t been good at all.” Pro Football Network ranks the Giants’ line 19th overall, 10th-best in the league blocking for the pass and just 30th for the run. Pro Football Focus ranks the Giants’ line sixth in pass-blocking, 31st in run-blocking. PFF has the Giants 15th overall. NFL Lines ranks the Giants 21st overall. The Giants are an average to slightly below league average line overall, and one of the better pass-blocking units in the NFL. There is no doubt they need to do a better job clearing holes for running backs. As for Jeff Stoutland, I have no idea whether or not he plans to return to coaching after this season. I would think he will have his choice of jobs, should he want to coach. I suppose it’s possible, but I don’t sense unhappiness with current offensive line coach Mike Bloomgren. Joe Castronova asks: Along with most Giant fans, and likely the rest of the NFL, Harbaugh’s leadership has been impressive. It stands out even more given the situation in Pittsburgh. What can you see is the primary difference between what we are getting with Harbaugh versus coaches in the past? Ed says: Joe, Harbaugh has brought a great many things to the Giants. His experience and previous success brought instant credibility. He brought an established way of doing things. Players understand who is in charge and what the standard is. There is no facade with Harbaugh. Everybody knows where they stand. Shoot, even I know where I stand with him. In my view, Joe Judge tried to be something he wasn’t — a Bill Belichick tough guy. Brian Daboll forgot that when you are the head coach you can’t be everybody’s buddy, and when things don’t go the way you want alienating your coaches isn’t great. Players believe what Harbaugh tells them, even if it isn’t always what they want to hear. Matthew Burns asks: We know Jameis is under contract for 2027. If JJ continues to win and show developmental progress, how high of a draft pick do you think the Giants will be asking for? And do you think there is a team or teams willing to pay that price? Ed says: Matthew, what willl happen this offseason is guesswork at this point. As of right now, I think the proper course of action is to trade McCarthy for the best haul of draft picks the Giants can get. Coul that change? Sure? Might John Harbaugh h

item.description: DENVER, COLORADO - AUGUST 02: Kyle Freeland #21 of the Colorado Rockies looks on after his first career complete game win in a game against the Kansas City Royals at Coors Field on August 02, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Kyle Cooper/Colorado Rockies/Getty Images) Good morning, Purple Row! Here’s what’s going on with the Colorado Rockies and the rest of Major League Baseball. 2026 Rockies Individual Performance of the Year I thought there was a real possibility that Cole Carrigg would take home his third consecutive Purple Row Award, but Kyle Freeland earned a rather convincing victory with 52% of the vote for his complete game against the Kansas City Royals on August 2 . On one of the hottest afternoons in Coors Field history, with the trade deadline looming the following day, Freeland took the mound for his 251st career start. There was a feeling it could be his last start in a Rockies uniform, but Freeland seemed unperturbed. The veteran southpaw gave Royals leadoff hitter Carter Jensen four different looks to open the game, putting him away with a knuckle curve. View Link The Royals scratched across their only run of the afternoon in the second inning when Luke Maile followed a John Rave single and a Josh Rojas walk with a two-out RBI single. Kansas City threatened again in the third when Jac Caglianone doubled with one out. Freeland moved the ball around the zone against Salvador Perez before burying consecutive knuckle curves, getting the veteran catcher to chase the second on a full count. View Link He retired Starling Marte on the very next pitch. Kansas City wouldn’t have another baserunner until the ninth. Freeland leaned into his cutter and sinker, inducing weak contact, and wasn’t shy about doubling up on his knuckle curve. He took different approaches against Maile and Jensen in the fifth, but put both away with consecutive curves before giving Nick Loftin five different looks and inducing a harmless fly ball. With the Rockies clinging to a 2-1 lead in the sixth, Brett Sullivan successfully challenged a knuckle curve at the bottom of the zone to strike out Marte and end the inning. item.content:encoded: DENVER, COLORADO - AUGUST 02: Kyle Freeland #21 of the Colorado Rockies looks on after his first career complete game win in a game against the Kansas City Royals at Coors Field on August 02, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Kyle Cooper/Colorado Rockies/Getty Images) Good morning, Purple Row! Here’s what’s going on with the Colorado Rockies and the rest of Major League Baseball. 2026 Rockies Individual Performance of the Year I thought there was a real possibility that Cole Carrigg would take home his third consecutive Purple Row Award, but Kyle Freeland earned a rather convincing victory with 52% of the vote for his complete game against the Kansas City Royals on August 2 . On one of the hottest afternoons in Coors Field history, with the trade deadline looming the following day, Freeland took the mound for his 251st career start. There was a feeling it could be his last start in a Rockies uniform, but Freeland seemed unperturbed. The veteran southpaw gave Royals leadoff hitter Carter Jensen four different looks to open the game, putting him away with a knuckle curve. View Link The Royals scratched across their only run of the afternoon in the second inning when Luke Maile followed a John Rave single and a Josh Rojas walk with a two-out RBI single. Kansas City threatened again in the third when Jac Caglianone doubled with one out. Freeland moved the ball around the zone against Salvador Perez before burying consecutive knuckle curves, getting the veteran catcher to chase the second on a full count. View Link He retired Starling Marte on the very next pitch. Kansas City wouldn’t have another baserunner until the ninth. Freeland leaned into his cutter and sinker, inducing weak contact, and wasn’t shy about doubling up on his knuckle curve. He took different approaches against Maile and Jensen in the fifth, but put both away with consecutive curves before giving Nick Loftin five different looks and inducing a harmless fly ball. With the Rockies clinging to a 2-1 lead in the sixth, Brett Sullivan successfully challenged a knuckle curve at the bottom of the zone to strike out Marte and end the inning. View Link The Rockies broke things open with a six-run sixth inning, and by then, Freeland was cruising. He dispatched the Royals on just eight pitches in the seventh, including a four-pitch strikeout of Tyler Tolbert. Zach Agnos began warming in the bullpen in the eighth, but Freeland retired the side in order once again. He had needed just 49 pitches to navigate five consecutive perfect innings. With 97 pitches under his belt, Freeland opened the ninth with his hardest pitch of the afternoon — a 92.4 mph fastball that Caglianone grounded to second. View Link It was the 18th consecutive batter Freeland had retired, a career high. A double from Perez and a single from Marte put runners on the corners with one out, and Agnos was warming once again. But Freeland worked out of trouble, inducing consecutive flyballs to Troy Johnston in right field. His 115th and final pitch was a 92.3 mph sinker. Freeland held the Royals to one run on five hits and two walks while striking out eight, securing an 8-1 victory, a series sweep and the first complete game of his career. If you’ve spent much time watching the Rockies over the past decade, chances are you’ve spent a fair amount of that time watching Kyle Freeland pitch. He’s started more games, pitched more innings and faced more batters than any pitcher in franchise history and is tied with Ubaldo Jiménez for the most pitching rWAR (18.9). Now a free agent, Freeland has likely pitched his final game for the Rockies. Asked if he had a message for the Rockies faithful following his complete game, Freeland kept it simple. “I love you guys. All ten years. I love you guys.” View Link After ten years of watching Kyle Freeland take the mound for the Rockies, I’m glad we get to celebrate this one. Rockies news and links The Guardians and Rockies are spending. It’s not because they fear a salary floor | The Athletic ($) Ken Rosenthal, Katie Woo and Will Sammon explore why two of baseball’s more frugal franchises are opening their wallets this winter. Among the more interesting nuggets is the role the Penners’ investment played in allowing the Rockies to build a rotation for the next several years. There’s also some insight into how the front office views the collective cost of acquiring Davis Martin, Patrick Sandoval and David Peterson. Perhaps that’s a better way of evaluating what the Rockies have done this winter than dissecting each acquisition individually. A Lesser-Known Prospect Who Will Help the Rockies in 2027 | Sports Illustrated Miguel Mike Medina highlights one of my favorite prospects outside of the Rockies’ top 10, Bryant Betancourt. The left-handed hitting catcher set career highs in home runs (17) and doubles (28) in 2026, posting an .816 OPS and earning a promotion to Triple-A. While I’m bullish on Betancourt, I think expecting him in Denver in 2027 might be a little ambitious. That said, the Rockies have some interesting catching prospects working their way through the system. Can Happ Give Rockies Boost in Outfield? | Roundtable Sports Joe Rutland explores the possibility of the Rockies signing free-agent outfielder Ian Happ. Despite hitting just .218 in 2026, the switch-hitting veteran hit 24 home runs and would bring good defense and some much-needed patience at the plate to Colorado. I like Happ as a player, but I’m not sure I like the fit as the roster is currently constructed. Of course, that could change considerably if the Rockies start dealing from their outfield depth. Around MLB Predicting Every MLB Team’s 2027 Opening Day Lineup With Signings and Trades | Bleacher Report Joel Reuter takes an early stab at projecting Opening Day lineups for all 30 MLB clubs, factoring in some hypothetical signings and trades along the way. While I think we have a pretty good idea of what the Rockies’ starting nine will look like, I was a little surprised to see Reuter pencil in Charlie Condon as Colorado’s Opening Day designated hitter. A little ambitious, perhaps, but I’m certainly here for it! Itoh, last of Big 3 from NPB, reaches deal with Cubs (source) | MLB.com The Cubs have been busy this winter. After committing $240 million to Trevor Rogers and Teruaki Sato, Chicago has reportedly reached an agreement with Japanese right-hander Hiromi Itoh. The 29-year-old posted a 3.18 ERA with a 4.7% walk rate across 172 ⅔ innings in 2026 after winning the Sawamura Award in 2025. Jordan Bastian also touches on the Cubs’ investment in scouting and developing relationships in Japan, something I’d love to see the Rockies put a greater emphasis on moving forward. Exemptions for ADHD drugs in MLB drop again to record-low 49 | Associated Press A somewhat curious headline given that the report offers little explanation as to why exemptions for ADHD medications continue to decline. What I found more interesting was that MLB administered a record 12,035 drug tests during the reporting period, with just three positive tests resulting in suspensions. Over the past five years, more than 57,000 tests have been administered, with just 15 positive tests resulting in suspensions. Quite a departure from the drug testing landscape of two decades ago. item.title: 3 Keys to Victory: Michigan Football at Ohio State
item.description: In the blink of an eye, Michigan’s season went from a complete and utter failure to what could be a similar story to the 2024 season. The Wolverines were 6-5 going into The Game in 2024, but the outlook on the season completely changed when it upset the No. 1 team in the country.Michigan’s 6-5 team of 2026 doesn’t have that exact same opportunity, but after beating then-No. 4 UCLA last week, it would feel similar if it capped the season off with a win over the Buckeyes. It’s the biggest game of the year, no matter the records or circumstances, as Michigan and Ohio State meet for the 122nd rendition of The Game. Here are the keys to victory for the Wolverines. Win the turnover margin Last week proved exactly why the turnover margin is so important in football, and how damaging it can be for a Michigan team that has struggled with that aspect of the game all season long. UCLA entered last Saturday with a +16 turnover margin, the best in the Big Ten and tied for second in the FBS. The Wolverines forced three turnovers and only turned it over once — the final takeaway leading to a game-altering touchdown at the beginning of the fourth quarter. Michigan is still last in the Big Ten with a -8 turnover margin, but Ohio State isn’t great either with a -3 turnover margin, tied for 14th in the conference. If it needs reminding, three of the Wolverines’ biggest wins — Week 2 against Oklahoma, Week 7 against Penn State, Week 11 against UCLA — have been the only games they won the turnover margin. One of the only faults of this Michigan defense has been its inability to force turnovers, but if last week was an indication of how The Game will go, it could be a long day for an Ohio State offense that has turned the ball over seven times in the last four games, three of which ended in losses. Keep a strong run game Freshman running back Savion Hiter had himself a game against the Bruins. For an offense that’s been struggling to find its footing all season long, especially in the run game, his performance proved something replicable. Hiter had a career-high 26 carries for 104 yards against UCLA, and it was his second consecutive game with more than 100 yards rushing. Ohio State has the 15th -best rushing defense in FBS, allowing just 100.3 yards per game. Even with the injuries and blunders of the Buckeyes’ offense, the defense has remained intact and hasn’t allowed more than 116 yards rushing to an opponent in the last four weeks, despite three of them ending in losses. If the Michigan offense can limit the negative run plays caused by blocking issues along the line, and rally behind Hiter and the run game to spark the offense, it may score just enough points to win. Continue making field goals The unsung heroes of Michigan’s win over UCLA was freshman kicker Jacob Baggett and punter Cam Brown, the latter of whom handled some difficult snaps as the holder. The Wolverines were 6-5 going into The Game in 2024, but the outlook on the season completely changed when it upset the No. 1 team in the country.Michigan’s 6-5 team of 2026 doesn’t have that exact same opportunity, but after beating then-No. 4 UCLA last week, it would feel similar if it capped the season off with a win over the Buckeyes. One of the only faults of this Michigan defense has been its inability to force turnovers, but if last week was an indication of how The Game will go, it could be a long day for an Ohio State offense that has turned the ball over seven times in the last four games, three of which ended in losses. Continue making field goals The unsung heroes of Michigan’s win over UCLA was freshman kicker Jacob Baggett and punter Cam Brown, the latter of whom handled some difficult snaps as the holder. Baggett made a 46-yard kick to score the game’s first points before nailing a 29-yarder and a 52-yarder in the overtime periods. The Wolverines were 5-for-11 on field goals going into last weekend against the Bruins, and 3-for-9 in Big Ten play. Missed field goals were one of the main contributors in failing to pull off the upset over then-No. 6 Indiana at home. But in the past few weeks, it seems Whittingham and the entire Michigan team is rallying behind their freshman kicker to get the job done when he’s needed. Ohio State has historically had some troubles kicking field goals in The Game — take 2024 for example when the Buckeyes were 1-for-3. So in what will likely be a low scoring game between two teams with very strong defenses, any points possible are going to be imperative to winning. Michigan might need to count on Baggett just like last weekend.

item.title: Chicago Cubs news — Sato, Shaw, Aguiar
item.description: Today’s Reflections Good morning, everyone. I hope everyone had a good Turkey Day, a calm period before the lockout deadline storm, and a special Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade today before the college football starts. I know this isn’t a college site. But I’ve occasionally heard the phrase, “Cheering for the laundry.” College football is in a deep part of my Sooner soul, alongside baseball. I can’t believe my having to do this after all these years — with all the NIL and portal over-usage, I have been doing nothing but cheering for the laundry of the Crimson and Cream. I only know the name of the QB, top WR and a few top tacklers. Why should I dig deep on the depth chart, or follow recruiting at all because a lot of those guys will be gone to the highest bidder? item.title: Rain, wind gusts up to 30 mph expected for 49ers-Seahawks showdown
item.description: Rain falls during the fourth quarter of an NFC Divisional Playoffs game between the Green Bay Packers and the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif., on Jan. 20, 2024. (Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) Sunday's pivotal matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and Seattle Seahawks is set to be played in wet and windy weather . In a phone interview with SFGATE on Friday, National Weather Service meteorologist Dial Hoang said rain is expected to hit the Bay Area on Sunday morning. The rain will likely roll in from the North Bay, where it's expected to arrive shortly after sunrise, and reach Santa Clara County and the area surrounding Levi's Stadium in the late morning. Once it arrives, it won't go away for the rest of the day, he said. "We're looking at the rain continuing across the Bay Area during the game, and especially after the game," Hoang told SFGATE. "Those lingering showers may extend into Monday morning." It shouldn't be overly cold - the forecast calls for temperatures to be in the mid-60s - and shouldn't rain too heavily, with around a quarter of an inch expected. But Hoang said it will be "gusty" during Sunday's game, with wind gusts expected to be between 25 and 30 mph. "It does look like the wind is going to be a strong factor," Hoang said. It's been a wet few weeks in the Bay Area, with a Nov. 18 storm breaking rainfall records in various Bay Area cities and causing flooding in several pockets of San Francisco. The region also saw near-historic high tides last week as part of the ongoing impact of El Niño this winter. The 49ers have already made several preparations in anticipation of a rainy winter. While the players and coaches were training in Colorado Springs, Colorado, to prepare for a game in Mexico City last week, the 49ers built a rain canopy over one of their practice fields in Santa Clara. Why does this now exist at #49ers HQ? Kyle Shanahan: "Because I keep getting told about El Niño or something" https://t.co/dh4iWI49Mk - Harrison Rich (@harrisonrich_) November 25, 2026 When asked during a news conference why the team opted to add the canopy, head coach Kyle Shanahan quipped, "Because I keep getting told about El Niño or something," before explaining its benefits, which can give the 49ers the closest thing to the bubble-like indoor facilities that many football teams have across the country. "Sometimes, when it's just like a monsoon out there and we're playing in a bubble, you can get a little bit more done with not being in that [rain]," Shanahan said. "So, if it ends up being like that, like people have warned, it's nice that at least we can walk through and stuff like that." It was sunny at the Niners' practice on Friday in Santa Clara, but the team is practicing with the rain in mind. With starting quarterback Brock Purdy out with an ankle injury, backup Mac Jones was spotted squirting water onto the football to help practice throwing a "wet ball," similar to what the team is expecting on Sunday.

item.title: UH's 'Old Man Club' prepares for final home game after 15 combined college football seasons
item.description: Brandon Mack II's eight-year college odyssey comes to an end with UH on Saturday. (Icon Sportswire/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) They've heard all the jokes about their age, how long they've played college football and all the changes they've witnessed. Meet defensive linemen Brandon Mack II and Quindario Lee, card-carrying members of the University of Houston' s unofficial "Old Man Club." When the No. 18 Cougars host Baylor for Senior Night on Saturday, two of the longest-tenured players in school history will play their final home game. Eight seasons for Mack. Seven seasons for Lee. UH vs. BAYLOR: How to watch "A lot of stories with those guys, a lot of memories," said James Ross III, the Cougars' edges and defensive run-game coordinator. Both are 25 years old. Mack goes by the nickname "Unc." Lee, who is three months older, is called "Gramps." "B-Mac always reminds me I'm older," Lee said with a laugh. And you'll likely never see their type of longevity again. The NCAA's new age-based eligibility model, which limits players to five seasons within a five-year window, will make it impossible to replicate careers that have combined for 15 seasons and spanned two presidential terms. "I'm just excited to see them transition into life," Ross said. He jokingly added, "We tried to find some more years. There are no more hidden years anywhere else." Sign up for Cougar Confidential You'll get get in-depth news and analysis about UH's basketball and football teams from reporter Joseph Duarte by signing up for the Cougar Confidential newsletter . While there is no official category, Mack and Lee are believed to be the longest-tenured players in program history. Their careers have been prolonged by an extra year of eligibility because of the COVID-19 pandemic and medical redshirts. A three-star defensive end out of high school, Mack signed with Ole Miss in 2018. He spent four seasons in Oxford, missing one with a foot injury, before transferring to UH in 2023. His first season with the Cougars ended prematurely, however, when he suffered a high-grade tear of the lat muscle on his left side in the second week of the season. He has been healthy the past three seasons, playing in 12 games in 2024 and set to play 13 games in consecutive seasons with the Cougars qualifying for a bowl. "I feel like yesterday was my first time in TDECU Stadium when we played UTSA and wore our powder blue jerseys," said Mack, who has posted 10 sacks over the past three seasons. "Then you blink and it's over. It definitely felt like it went by fast." Mack thought his college career was over last November. He began filling out information for the Cougars' Senior Night ceremony when he was told he had another year of eligibility. Lee's path has been just as winding. A three-year defensive lineman, Lee went from small-town Alabama to Fort Scott (Kan.) Community College. He transferred to Central Michigan, where he played 24 games over three seasons, before arriving at UH in 2024.

(Icon Sportswire/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) They've heard all the jokes about their age, how long they've played college football and all the changes they've witnessed. UH vs. BAYLOR: How to watch "A lot of stories with those guys, a lot of memories," said James Ross III, the Cougars' edges and defensive run-game coordinator. Both are 25 years old. Mack goes by the nickname "Unc." Lee, who is three months older, is called "Gramps." "B-Mac always reminds me I'm older," Lee said with a laugh. And you'll likely never see their type of longevity again. The NCAA's new age-based eligibility model, which limits players to five seasons within a five-year window, will make it impossible to replicate careers that have combined for 15 seasons and spanned two presidential terms. "I'm just excited to see them transition into life," Ross said. He jokingly added, "We tried to find some more years. There are no more hidden years anywhere else." Sign up for Cougar Confidential You'll get get in-depth news and analysis about UH's basketball and football teams from reporter Joseph Duarte by signing up for the Cougar Confidential newsletter . While there is no official category, Mack and Lee are believed to be the longest-tenured players in program history. Their careers have been prolonged by an extra year of eligibility because of the COVID-19 pandemic and medical redshirts. A three-star defensive end out of high school, Mack signed with Ole Miss in 2018. He spent four seasons in Oxford, missing one with a foot injury, before transferring to UH in 2023. His first season with the Cougars ended prematurely, however, when he suffered a high-grade tear of the lat muscle on his left side in the second week of the season. He has been healthy the past three seasons, playing in 12 games in 2024 and set to play 13 games in consecutive seasons with the Cougars qualifying for a bowl. "I feel like yesterday was my first time in TDECU Stadium when we played UTSA and wore our powder blue jerseys," said Mack, who has posted 10 sacks over the past three seasons. "Then you blink and it's over. It definitely felt like it went by fast." Mack thought his college career was over last November. He began filling out information for the Cougars' Senior Night ceremony when he was told he had another year of eligibility. Lee's path has been just as winding. A three-year defensive lineman, Lee went from small-town Alabama to Fort Scott (Kan.) Community College. He transferred to Central Michigan, where he played 24 games over three seasons, before arriving at UH in 2024. Lee played 12 games in his first season but eventually needed back surgery and missed last season with a wrist injury. "I had a long journey," said Lee, who has 1½ sacks this season in a reserve role. "I've seen everything." That includes the transformation of college football, from the transfer portal to NIL (name, image and likeness) and revenue sharing, which now allows players to be paid. Mack went from the SEC - which at the time didn't include Texas or Oklahoma - to the American Athletic Conference and Big 12. "Nowadays, it's very easy to become selfish when things don't go your way," Ross said. "To see those two guys, in particular, just be team guys and stay the course and bring wisdom to the group ... for those guys to be dedicated as they were throughout this whole journey was awesome to see. They definitely helped set the foundation for where we are right now." On a couple of occasions, both players considered calling it quits. "My family got me through it," said Mack, who has a team-high 8½ tackles for loss. "A lot of times I thought about how my body wasn't agreeing with me and things weren't going my way. I wanted to, but my family was in my corner telling me to keep going. Once I got that first season out of the way, it became more about telling myself, ‘Keep going. I've got something to finish.'" That includes the chance for the Cougars to post consecutive 10-win seasons for the first time in school history. "Our goal is to win every game that we play," Mack said. "We're going to try and make that happen." Lee said the relationships he has formed with coaches and teammates will last a lifetime. He calls Mack his "best friend." "The friendships, just the bonds," Lee said of his best memories. "These guys are my brothers." As the Cougars went through practices this week, Mack and Lee said the emotions began to set in as their college careers neared an end. "I'm trying to really just take it in, just soak it in and enjoy these last few weeks," Lee said. What advice would Mack give himself nearly a decade later? "You're going to face challenges. Just keep going," he said. "Don't get down on yourself. When things aren't looking bright, just look up and keep pushing. Life is all about challenges and getting through challenges." item.title: Panthers vs Buccaneers: Matchups to watch
item.description: CHARLOTTE, NC - OCTOBER 25: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Bucky Irving (7) begins the celebration after scoring a touchdown during an NFL football game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Carolina Panthers on October 25, 2026 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have a chance to plant themselves firmly in the drivers seat of the NFC South. They have a two game lead over every other team in the division, and right now the Buccaneers are the only team that have a chance to take the head to head tiebreaker over them. Taking a three game lead over the Bucs while also clinching not being on the wrong side of any head to head tiebreakers almost seems insurmountable given how hard it is for NFC South teams to win any games. That said, the last time these teams played was a complete catastrophe for the Panthers. They squandered away the home leg of the home-and-home with a performance featuring mistakes by every unit. They practically invented ways for things to go wrong, all the while they couldn’t stop either Buccaneers running back from gaining like 10 yards before making an attempt at tackling them. That first meeting is going to provide us with a little bit of a guide for where we’ll focus this matchups post. Panthers front seven vs Bucky Irving Bucky Irving has always been a nightmare for the Panthers. He averages over 100 rushing yards per game against Carolina for his career. The first meeting was no different. He finished with 106 yards on 24 carries, but that somewhat undersells how badly the Panthers struggled with him. He gained yardage on virtually every carry; he just didn’t have any long enough gains to boost his yards per carry. He’s had a couple of those games this year and is sneakily fourth in the NFL in rushing yards. The Panthers have to do a much better job of clogging up his run lanes and wrapping him before he has a chance to get into space, where he becomes nearly impossible to get down with just one guy. Panthers interior offensive line vs Vita Vea and Calijah Kancey The Panthers have had their issues blocking for Bryce Young up front. Luke Fortner has been a weak spot at center and Robert Hunt hasn’t been his old self. Vita Vea and Calijah Kancey are both top 20 in ESPN’s pass rush win rate for defensive tackles. They’re part of a Tampa Bay defense that’s becoming a very formidable unit as the season goes on. Young obviously has problems with interior pressure given his short stature. A night of Vea and Kancey disrupting the middle of the pocket is going to make it very hard for the Panthers offense to move the ball. They’re going to need Fortner and Hunt to step up and play better than they have to this point in the season. Jaelan Phillips vs Luke Goedeke Phillips has been a major disruptor since he returned a couple of weeks ago. The Buccaneers have an elite pair of offensive tackles and a very good offensive line on the whole. Phillips needs to keep up his disruptive ways, both in the run game and the pass game. He’s going to be a key component of keeping Irving from getting out into space. He’s also going to have to get pressure on Baker Mayfield, who hasn’t been good this season, in passing situations. Carolina Panthers vs Themselves In the first game, the Panthers were behind 7-0, but they had forced the Buccaneers into a quick punt. David Moore muffed that punt, which set the Bucs up for a free field goal. On the Panthers’ next possession, Young was sacked and lost the ball, which was scooped up for another Buccaneers score. Those two turnovers in rapid succession was the jolt that knocked the wheels off, and the Panthers never recovered. The margins have been small for Carolina this season. They need to keep the train on the tracks this time around and make the Buccaneers beat them possession after possession.

item.title: “Caitlin Clark Has Actual MOTION” – Fans Absolutely Love Kate Martin’s Story About Aussie Vet Kelly Wilson Embracing Fever Star’s Signature Shoe
item.description: LA Sparks vs. Indiana Fever - 2026 WNBA regular season © Imagn Images Kate Martin has started the next chapter of her basketball career in Australia’s WNBL. While it’s a long way from her country of origin, Martin’s basketball ties to the U.S. remain strong. On Friday’s episode of the “Cut to the Jase” podcast, the former Iowa Hawkeyes guard told a story about her Bendigo Spirit teammate Kelly Wilson enjoying the signature shoe of her ex-college running mate, Caitlin Clark. “My teammate has been playing for 20 years and has never worn basketball shoes. But the CC 1s, she loves them. She’s been rocking them. Caitlin’s response was, ‘That makes my whole world.’ And now, she’s like, ‘Tell me what colorway Kelly wants. I’m gonna send them to her.'” After hearing the story, fans had positive things to say about Clark, Martin, and the Caitlin 1s. “Caitlin Clark has actual MOTION!!” one fan tweeted . Clark and Martin have not had the chance to team up in the WNBA, but from the looks of it, they’ve kept in touch. At the same time, Martin’s story is a testament to the popularity of her friend’s signature shoe. From Australia to the United States and everywhere else in between, Clark’s Caitlin 1s have been a smash hit since they were released in October. “I’ve Never Seen Anybody Doing the Things That She’s Doing”: Kate Martin Recalls Caitlin Clark Showcasing Her Skills in College In the same podcast appearance, Kate Martin opened up on her first impressions of Caitlin Clark. According to Martin, she wasn’t sure about her then-teammate’s capabilities at first. “I remember her coming in, and I was like, this freshman’s gonna think she’s the bee’s knees or whatever…The first week of practice, I was like, I’ve never seen anybody doing the things that she’s doing.” Martin also explained that when fans accused the Hawkeyes of not being happy for Clark’s stellar play on the court, it was because she and her teammates had already seen CC hit logo 3s and pull off other amazing feats in practice. On Friday’s episode of the “Cut to the Jase” podcast, the former Iowa Hawkeyes guard told a story about her Bendigo Spirit teammate Kelly Wilson enjoying the signature shoe of her ex-college running mate, Caitlin Clark. “My teammate has been playing for 20 years and has never worn basketball shoes. But the CC 1s, she loves them. She’s been rocking them. Caitlin’s response was, ‘That makes my whole world.’ And now, she’s like, ‘Tell me what colorway Kelly wants. I’m gonna send them to her.'” After hearing the story, fans had positive things to say about Clark, Martin, and the Caitlin 1s. “Caitlin Clark has actual MOTION!!” one fan tweeted . Clark and Martin have not had the chance to team up in the WNBA, but from the looks of it, they’ve kept in touch. At the same time, Martin’s story is a testament to the popularity of her friend’s signature shoe. From Australia to the United States and everywhere else in between, Clark’s Caitlin 1s have been a smash hit since they were released in October. “I’ve Never Seen Anybody Doing the Things That She’s Doing”: Kate Martin Recalls Caitlin Clark Showcasing Her Skills in College In the same podcast appearance, Kate Martin opened up on her first impressions of Caitlin Clark. According to Martin, she wasn’t sure about her then-teammate’s capabilities at first. “I remember her coming in, and I was like, this freshman’s gonna think she’s the bee’s knees or whatever…The first week of practice, I was like, I’ve never seen anybody doing the things that she’s doing.” Martin also explained that when fans accused the Hawkeyes of not being happy for Clark’s stellar play on the court, it was because she and her teammates had already seen CC hit logo 3s and pull off other amazing feats in practice. Eight years in the making, Balser, 35, hoped to beat the previous record set by Pete Kostelnick, who ran from San Francisco City Hall to N.Y.C. in 42 days in 2016. The determined athlete was able to do so, beating Kostelnick by 13 hours and 45 minutes. Following the feat, Balser, 35, opened up to PEOPLE about what the run means to him, what some of the hardest parts were and how he leaned on Kostelnick to keep himself grounded in why he wanted to take this on in the first place. “Running’s always been something I’ve been very passionate about. I just didn’t know where that was gonna go. I ran some more ultramarathons and I met Pete, who had the record, and got to talk to him about his trip across the country,” Balser says. “That influenced me to want to run around America. In 2023, I ran the perimeter of the United States. I did a solo thing and I ran 11,170 miles in 294 days around America. After that, it kinda gave me a good resume for people to wanna kinda back me.” Cameron Balser running across America Credit: Alessandro Portante For the Trans America Run, Balser was sponsored by Mount to Coast . item.content:encoded: Cameron Balser running Credit: Alessandro Portante NEED TO KNOW Cameron Balser broke the Trans America Run record, running 3,000 miles in 41 days across 12 states Balser faced physical, mental, and safety challenges, including traffic dangers and running up to 16 hours daily He credits his support team and community for helping him achieve his goal and inspire others through his journey After 41 days and over 3,000 miles, ultramarathoner Cameron Balser reached New York City Hall to set a new record for the Trans America Run on Friday, Nov. 20. Eight years in the making, Balser, 35, hoped to beat the previous record set by Pete Kostelnick, who ran from San Francisco City Hall to N.Y.C. in 42 days in 2016. The determined athlete was able to do so, beating Kostelnick by 13 hours and 45 minutes. Following the feat, Balser, 35, opened up to PEOPLE about what the run means to him, what some of the hardest parts were and how he leaned on Kostelnick to keep himself grounded in why he wanted to take this on in the first place. “Running’s always been something I’ve been very passionate about. I just didn’t know where that was gonna go. I ran some more ultramarathons and I met Pete, who had the record, and got to talk to him about his trip across the country,” Balser says. “That influenced me to want to run around America. In 2023, I ran the perimeter of the United States. I did a solo thing and I ran 11,170 miles in 294 days around America. After that, it kinda gave me a good resume for people to wanna kinda back me.” Cameron Balser running across America Credit: Alessandro Portante For the Trans America Run, Balser was sponsored by Mount to Coast . He started his race in San Francisco on Saturday, Oct. 10 before crossing 12 states over 41 consecutive days, climbing more than 42,000 meters and averaging 72.1 miles per day. Some days, he spent up to 16 hours running. “The team would wake me up around 4:25, 4:30. I would wake up then and have 10 minutes to slam some food and try to wake myself up. By 5:00 a.m. almost every day, we would start running,” Balser says. Every five miles, he says he would “eat literally as much as I could.” “Then I would go back out there and the team would be looking for anything that would need water, food and stuff like that. Running from 5:00 a.m. to basically 9:00 p.m. every night and then 10 minutes I would have a little bit of a wind down and then I would go to sleep and I did that for basically 41 days straight,” Balser reflects. Prior to the run, Balser worked on a regenerative farm and got used to the long hours. After the farm work, he would run 25 to 30 miles a week, and then on weekends would run 40 to 50 miles. “I was more prepared than I thought. We were very lucky and fortunate that it literally felt like miracle after miracle was unfolding in front of us,” Balser says. Balser says the most surprising aspect was spending up to 16 hours every day with himself, with him reaching a moment where he felt like he had “nothing else to give.” However, what changed his mindset was when his friend, Sam, told him to “let the love in.” “That moment after that it felt like everything was unfolding more than I could imagine. It was like I was keeping something. I had a little bit more to let go, and it was a big thing to let go, and I can just feel that energy of love, and that’s what was most important about this trip was showing how good it is to love yourself with the people around you and follow what you’re truly passionate about,” Balser says. Cameron Balser and a group running at night Credit: Alessandro Portante Along the route, people would join him and run segments with him. “We had the people we needed at the right place at the right time. We had teammates, fly in and come and help us as well. Whatever time they had to give, they gave,” he says. “As we got to Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, all the way to New York City, I hardly ran any days alone. I had a few days in Pennsylvania, but there was always somebody coming out, especially if they’re local, they were telling us everything about their city and how happy they were, and proud they were of the city,” Balser recalls. The biggest challenge about the run, however, was “myself,” he says.“Everything else was taken care of. I wrote down a lot of things I wanted for the trip, and everything I ever could have dreamed of was right in front of me. I was like, ‘Dude, there’s nothing you have to worry about other than running.’ ” Then, whenever he had a low moment and he found himself fighting with his own ego, “I was just like, ‘What do people think of me if I can’t run, if I have to walk this in?’ ” he says, noting that his team supported him and let him know that if he had to walk it in, that’s what they would do. The other challenge that he faced was traffic. Balser, who wore a safety vest during his trek, says that “75% of the time” he was “watching for cars, and someone on their phone or just not paying attention.” “I encountered almost dying every day, so that was a lot. I was focused on the next step I was taking and trying to be as present as I could be. I lost my vision day by day and I had nothing more I could focus on rather than what was in front of me or I would get myself in a position where I was looking too far ahead or looking back too much,” Balser says. Cameron Balser and his van Credit: Alessandro Portante Not only that, but Balser had to put on music or listen to a show on Netflix to drown out the noise of the passing cars — all while he tried to maintain his safety. “There was a good portion where, when the traffic was insane, I had to drown that out, which as crazy as it sounds, if I didn’t, I felt like I could have PTSD from just hearing cars go past me at 75 miles per hour in the middle of Nebraska or Iowa,” he says. He notes, “I listened to everything you could think of, and I thought of every thought you could think of, probably a thousand times until my brain would go dead. I knew if you can’t see them, they can’t see you.” Helping to keep him safe was his team, a support crew following him in a van, who sometimes would have people run with him. He also credits the people who cheered him along the way. Cameron Balser in New York City Credit: Alessandro Portante Every day, he would try to get about six hours of sleep, and that’s where most of his recovery would come from. If there was a hotel within five miles of where he stopped running, he and his team would stay there. Most of the time, however, they slept in the van. When Balser had completed his run, he didn’t expect to be greeted by such a large crowd of people. “I felt like this is really what the world is about and this is the world I wanna live in. I saw so many smiling faces and I stayed after and hugged everybody that came out there,” he says. “It’s something I’ll never forget and I will always know if you put everything into a day or into your life, there’s nothing you can’t do. I’m just gonna love this experience more and more and more and more. Whatever I can do to help other people, that’s what I’m gonna do, I’m just grateful,” Balser continues. Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. Now that the run is finished, Balser is focusing on recovery and continues to give himself the love that he needs. He hopes to inspire people with his story, saying, “I’m glad to show people if you go out there and it’s something that really aligns with you and it’s not anything out of ego and it’s just out of love, like, there’s really nothing you can’t do.” While he was the person physically running, he says, “I couldn’t have done it without everybody.” Balser adds, “Without people praying for me and people along the way that came out and helped us with certain things, doing laundry or getting us food.
